Container.d: A running, isolated copy of an application together with the exact libraries and settings it needs, started from a container image. Throwing a container away doesn't change the image it came from.

Container image.d: A read-only package of an application and everything it needs to run, built from a Dockerfile. The same image is tested, stored in a registry and run in production.

Docker Compose.d: A Docker tool that describes how to run one or more containers together, with their settings, secrets, ports and volumes, in a single YAML file such as compose.yaml.

Container registry.d: A server that stores container images so that pipelines and servers can push and pull them, for example GitHub's ghcr.io or Docker Hub.

Reverse proxy.d: A server that sits in front of an application, receives requests from users (often over HTTPS) and forwards them to the application. Caddy and nginx are common examples.

Health check.d: A small, cheap request that tells a machine whether an application is working, used to restart broken containers or decide whether a new version can take traffic.

Readiness check.d: A health check that asks whether an application can serve real requests right now (for example, whether its database and settings are in place), as opposed to merely being alive.

Rollback.d: Returning a system to the previous known-good version after a bad release. It restores code, not data, so back up before every release.

Continuous deployment.d: Automatically building and releasing every change that passes the tests, through a pipeline rather than by hand, often with an approval step before production.

Role-based access control.d: A way of managing permissions where each permission belongs to a role (such as viewer, tester or admin) and each user is given a role. Often shortened to RBAC.
